source_refs.note: Topic 1.9.1, printed pages 16-17: basic, amphoteric and acidic oxides with the printed equations, and Quick Check 1.8(a) as the self-check.

blocks.text: Oxides are binary compounds formed by the reaction of oxygen with other elements. They are classified by their characteristics as neutral, basic, amphoteric or acidic.

items: Basic oxides: an oxide that gives an alkali when combined with water. Metals react with oxygen to give basic oxides, which are usually ionic; groups 1 and 2 form them, for example Na2O, CaO and BaO. Na2O(s) + H2O(l) gives 2NaOH(aq); CaO(s) + H2O(l) gives Ca(OH)2(aq). The solubility of the group 2 hydroxides increases down the group, so their alkalinity increases down the group too.

Amphoteric oxides: oxides that react with both acids and bases, behaving as acid or base according to the conditions. Aluminium oxide (Al2O3) is insoluble in water but reacts with hydrochloric acid to form aluminium chloride and water, and with sodium hydroxide to form sodium aluminate and water: Al2O3(s) + 6HCl(aq) gives 2AlCl3(s) + 3H2O(l); Al2O3(s) + 2NaOH(aq) gives Na2Al2O4(s) + H2O(l).

Acidic oxides: an oxide that gives an acid when combined with water. Non-metals react with oxygen to form acidic oxides held together by covalent bonds; silicon dioxide counts as acidic because it reacts with bases. The acidic oxides of period 3 are P2O3, P2O5, SO3 and SO2. With water: P2O3(s) + H2O(l) gives H3PO3(aq); SO2(g) + H2O(l) gives H2SO3(aq). With bases: SiO2(s) + 2NaOH(aq) gives Na2SiO3(aq) + H2O(l); P2O3(s) + 6NaOH(aq) gives 2Na3PO3(aq) + 3H2O(l); SO2(g) + 2NaOH(aq) gives Na2SO3(aq) + H2O(l).
